Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace Squarespace: Share your passion with the world What are you afraid of?
Spiders? Public speaking? The dentist? Calculus? What about death? How you feel about death has probably been shaped by your beliefs about whether or not there’s an afterlife – and if there is, what it’s like. The ancient Egyptians believed that, at death,
your heart would be weighed against a feather, to determine if it was fit to enter the underworld. A heart heavy with mis-deeds would be fed
to a demon. Christians may envision Saint Peter, waiting
at the pearly gates to welcome you into heaven, unless your name doesn’t make his list. Imagine not only being turned away from the coolest club in town, but banished to the eternal torments of hell. As we learned in our discussions about the philosophy of religion, when the stakes are eternal, it’s only reasonable to get a little nervous about what’s basically the Ultimate Final Exam. But if it makes you feel any better, many
philosophers have believed, and still believe, that death is nothing to fear. [Theme Music] In 399 BCE, Socrates was sentenced to death
for, among other things, refusing to acknowledge the official deities
of Athens, radicalizing youth, and generally honking
off the people in charge. But even when he faced his own imminent death,
he remained calm and unafraid. He was a philosopher, after all.
And fear was no match for his ability to argue. Socrates didn’t think we could know if there’s
an afterlife or not, but he thought there were really only two
possibilities. And as far as he was concerned, neither of
them was anything to be afraid of. Here’s his argument: Either death is a dreamless sleep
Or death is a passage to another life Dreamless sleeps are nice, not scary
(Socrates said he could use the rest) And a passage to another life sounds good,
too, because he’ll get to hang out with cool
people from the past who have already died Therefore, either way, death is nothing to
fear Socrates’ idea of the afterlife was Hades, which he seems to have pictured as being a lot like Athens, except that no one had any physical bodies
– only disembodied minds. And frankly he thought that sounded awesome,
because bodies can be a real pain; they just need to be fed, and require rest.
Just, so much upkeep. So, in the afterlife, Socrates imagined he’d
get to have endless philosophical conversations, and continue learning new things, with the
greatest thinkers of the past. And they wouldn’t have to take a break to
eat or sleep or pee! Now, Socrates recognized that, although his favorite activity, philosophizing, didn’t require a body, some things do. And if all of your favorite pastimes are physical,
you might find the afterlife disappointing. That’s why Socrates recommended spending
your life looking after your mind, cultivating that part of you that you’ll
get to keep forever – if there’s an afterlife. If you do that, when the time comes for you
to die, you’ll actually see death as a benefit, because you won’t be troubled by bodily
things, while your mind will be in top form. But what if there isn’t an afterlife? What about that “dreamless sleep” that
Socrates spoke about? Isn’t total annihilation of the self, like,
the scariest thing there is? Ancient Stoic philosopher Epicurus didn’t
think so. He lived about a hundred years after Socrates,
and he rejected belief in an afterlife altogether. Instead, he said we’re just our bodies,
and nothing more. But still, he still didn’t find death scary. Here’s his argument.
Death is the cessation of sensation. Good and evil only make sense in terms of
sensation. So, Death is neither good nor evil. Epicurus was convinced that things are only
evil, or bad, if they feel bad. And he didn’t mean only physical feelings. Anyone who’s ever had a broken heart will tell you that it’s a lot more painful, and harder to heal, than a broken leg. But a broken heart is still a sensation – you
need a body to experience it – so as a materialist – someone who believed that You equal Your Body
– death just meant nonexistence. And there was nothing scary about that, because,
well, there won’t be any you to have any feelings
about not existing! Epicurus argued that fearing nonexistence is not only stupid, but it gets in the way of enjoying life. You are alive, and experiencing sensations,
now. So, he said, make those sensations as great
as possible, and don’t worry about when those sensations
are going to stop! YOLO! To help you understand Epicurus and his attitudes
about death a little better, let’s head over to the Thought Bubble for
some Flash Philosophy. Think about a hangover. If you haven’t had
one, imagine what they might be like. Hangovers aren’t bad for you before you
get one, right? In fact, the thing that comes before the hangover
is often quite pleasant, what with all the laughing, and feeling uninhibited, and working up the courage to talk to that cutie from your calculus class. No, the hangover is only bad while it’s
happening. And true: It might be bad after it’s over, like, if it kept you from doing well on your calculus exam the next morning, because you were too busy trying not to barf
in front of said cutie. But the point is, if something is bad for you, it’s generally bad for you at a particular time, the way a hangover is. But Epicurus said that death can’t be bad
for you at any time. Because once it arrives, you’re gone! The thing that eventually kills you? Yeah, that’s gonna be bad for you, before your death. But that’s not death. When you think about it, you and Death are
never present at the same time. And if there’s no you when death is present, then there is no time in which death is bad for you. Thanks, Thought Bubble! So, things like hangovers and charley horses and movie spoilers are bad, because you’re there to experience them. But as far as Epicurus was concerned, life
was like a night of drinking before a hangover, which – inevitable as it is –
you will never actually experience.

Death: Fear or Opportunity? A Debate on Mortality

This video explores different perspectives on death. It examines the fear associated with death and considers its potential impact on individuals' understanding of themselves.

Socrates and His Approach to Death

Ancient Greek philosopher Socrates believed there was no need to fear death, assuming that it could be either a "dreamless sleep" (a state of oblivion) or a passage to another life. He thought an afterlife might involve philosophical conversations with those who lived before him, in a world free from physical needs and constraints.

Epicurus and a Matter of Materialism

In contrast to Socrates' perspective, Epicurus, another ancient philosopher, believed the cessation of sensation is death itself. He stated that fear and anxiety associated with death are unfounded because experiencing life with all its sensations and positive experiences (such as working up courage) shouldn’t be hampered by a fear of the end.

Facing the Fears through an Epicurean Lens

Epicurus proposed that, rather than dwelling on what follows death, focus on enjoying the present moment. This involves appreciating life's joys and embracing sensations without worrying about their ultimate duration (life being akin to pre-hangover bliss). Death is considered a neutral state of nonexistence and therefore doesn't bring any negative experience.

Socrates' Perspective on Death

Socrates faced execution in 399 BCE for societal defiance and philosophical questioning. He maintained composure amidst his impending death due to a dedication to logic and reason rather than fear. Socrates believed in two possible outcomes after death: dreamless sleep or a passage to another life. He argued that neither scenario was inherently terrifying, suggesting even the concept of "nothingness" wouldn't be an impediment to a fruitful existence. He imagined an afterlife as reminiscent of Athens - devoid of physicality except for the disembodied minds. For Socrates, contemplation played a key role in his life; after death, he proposed, it would continue. This perspective on pursuing intellectual pursuits and cultivating one's mind provided a pathway to enduring value. While acknowledging that certain "physical pursuits" could be valuable as part of life, Socrates highlighted the need to protect these activities during life to ensure their preservation within an afterlife. For those struggling through challenging times, he suggested prioritizing the mental aspects to prepare for death and alleviate anxiety associated with it. A contrasting perspective was offered by Epicurus, a philosopher who lived centuries later. He rejected the concept of an afterlife, emphasizing the material existence (body) as the primary reality, devoid of any spiritual dimensions. Despite this belief, Epicurus did not find death itself threatening. This material view of life stemmed from the notion that death was simply the cessation of sensation(s), and therefore didn't present a threat that should impact one's mental state as death is merely nonexistence, which does not inherently entail any negative feelings or experiences. Epicurus proposed "living in the present moment," where enjoying the sensations one senses during life. The philosophical lens shifted to considering modern interpretations of living beyond our physical forms and how this shapes one's mortality fears. Thomas Nagel explored human perspectives on death. He argued that while many dread missing crucial life experiences - like game completion, book launches, or even the moon landing, these missed opportunities wouldn’t affect life as long it was lived in its true form. It appears to be a consequence of this individual's experience. Ultimately, the question emerges: How does one determine what truly defines "worth living for" amidst this complexity? The passage explores different philosophical approaches to understanding death.

Life after Death and Fear of Death 
Philosophers have contemplated the nature of life, death, and mortality for centuries. Socrates believed in an afterlife filled with philosophical discussions but acknowledged the importance of engaging in physical pursuits. He urged cultivating one's mind as preparation for death. Epicurus advocated for material existence and a focus on enjoyment during life, arguing that fearing nonexistence is irrational due to death's absence impacting experience.

In contrast, Thomas Nagel highlighted instances of FOMO (fear of missing out), where individuals may fear not experiencing the entire breadth of life before their death.  While there may be significant regret at passing away prematurely, if humans can live for roughly 80 years, some deaths are significant due to lost potential.

Philosophers hold differing opinions on what constitutes a "good" life - some believing in its inherent value; others valuing quality of experience over simple existence itself. Such beliefs influence how one perceives death's impact and the importance it holds regarding suffering versus loss.

### Epicurus' Perspective on Death 

This section examines Epicurus' philosophy on death and its connection to living a fulfilling life. He believed that:

* **Death is a cessation of sensation:**  Rather than being "good" or "bad," it simply means the end of the physical experience.
* **Death as nonexistence:** Epicurus considered materialist views, wherein one's self was solely comprised of their body, to be the only relevant explanation for death. He saw nothing inherently alarming about this lack of a physical form and believed death should not be feared. 

This philosophical thought contributed to Epicurus' belief that embracing sensory experiences is key: 
* **"YOLO": Live in the Present:**  He encouraged living for enjoyment rather than worrying about what will happen after death since life only exists at present moment and no experience of death would bring negativity into being; ultimately, it was simply nonexistence. 

### The Value in Experiences during Life  

The section explores how experiences, both pleasurable and challenging, contribute to the meaning we find in our existence:
* **Hangovers as a metaphor:** Epicurus used hangovers as an analogy for dealing with inevitable hardships in life- which will ultimately be meaningless. His point is that these hardships should not impede one's ability to enjoy their present life 

The  arguments presented here connect to a philosophical debate about the value of life and its interconnectedness to death:

* **Loss vs. Progress:** For some, mourning the loss of someone is seen as inevitable but also painful; others feel it is an important part of letting go.  There are different perspectives.


### Shifting Perspectives on Death: Mortality & Loss

This section explores the fear surrounding death specifically in the context  of loved ones.
* **Philosophical Debates:** There were philosophical debates and perspectives to how fear about a loved one's passing is illogical from the perspective that death will happen regardless of personal mourning and grief, 

**Zhuangzi’s View** on Death as Embracement: 

Here's what philosopher Zhuangzi (a follower of Epicurus) has to say about  death.


* **Acceptance & Celebration:** He believed it is foolish to mourn the loss of someone who will ultimately pass away; rather, a celebration or acceptance should be practiced over these times. He compared death to natural life and its progression as a cycle of birth, growth, change, and moving on for the same reason one may celebrate birthdays, bar mitzvahs, and graduations.. 



**Summary**:
The philosophy explored in this analysis  highlights an overall appreciation of living a more fulfilling existence; it emphasizes not fearing death itself but focusing on life's present moments and appreciating the unique experiences that we enjoy today. It also sheds light on different perspectives regarding mortality, offering a unique take on what we should expect when a loved one passes.

While hangovers are a momentary unpleasant situation that causes inconvenience, they're generally only bad at specific points during their occurrence. Death is an inevitability, but it isn't always experienced as something negative until after it happens because once death arrives we cease to exist.  Epicurus argues that life has the ability to provide meaning and enjoyment even in the face of challenges.

Epicurus compared a typical life’s experience to that of a night of drinking; enjoyable moments are followed by a temporary hangover effect. He viewed death as something separate from our normal existence, not inherently bad at any moment but experienced so as part of a larger cycle (though it can be impactful and even tragic). 

Philosopher Thomas Nagel suggests people often fear death because they are concerned about missing out on life’s experiences, creating what could be described as “fear of missing out” or FOMO.   They have this concern that by dying before finishing major tasks like video games or books written later.  Nagel argues if you didn't feel sadness at the potential missed moments because you lived such a short time, then there's no reason to mourn the passing of your life.

However, philosopher Thomas Nagel highlights how death should matter, even when it occurs early, as this loss is impactful in that person's absence from their loved ones and their existence was valuable or precious.  But some individuals believe quality of life matters more than just living without much of a purpose and therefore may value the passing if the event leads to happiness and fulfillment within an individual’s lifespan.

Other philosophers, such as Zhuangzi, propose we don't focus on death as it comes. A major philosophical concept was when someone dies it is viewed as part of a natural growth cycle or life in society.  As time passes, each milestone marks a stage, and these things should not cause unnecessary concern during the transition of passing from one stage into another. Death should not be seen as more of an obstacle to overcome because there's nothing wrong with moving along toward what could also be considered a "change". 
     
Finally, philosopher Zhuangzi suggests a shift in perspective when it comes to death is to focus on the beauty and joy that we have throughout life rather than sorrow and anxiety. Death is not something to fear but instead an exciting new beginning, as those around us will carry on with their own lives once they pass.
